title: Where do first names come from?

entries.note: Has meant name for all time; nearly every Proto-Indo-European language has a similar word beginning with N, with an M sound, related to [[same-root:nomenclature]].
Discussed in the hosts' earlier episode about -nym words.
Discussed in the hosts' earlier episode about -nym words.
Comes from the same Proto-Indo-European root, roughly nomen, meaning name, as [[same-root:name]].
A Germanic compound meaning bright and famous; the Norman form dropped the initial H found in other Germanic variants, and -bert is related to [[same-root:bright]].
Directly related to the -bert ending of [[same-root:Robert]], [[same-root:Albert]] and similar names.
Means noble bright, with the same -bert ending as [[same-root:Robert]].
Means mind bright, with the same -bert ending as [[same-root:Robert]].
Means bright sword, from Old English [[from:ecg]], the source of edge, which also meant sword; Rob finds it surprisingly kick-ass.
An Anglo-Saxon name meaning wolf stone, borne by an English Benedictine monk.
An Anglo-Saxon name meaning warrior wolf, borne by a king of Mercia.
A common element in Anglo-Saxon names; in Old English it could also mean a genius, someone supernaturally intelligent, as in [[see:Alfred]].
Ultimately means elf council, where [[see:elf]] meant something like genius.
Means army commander; its ending means strong, as in [[same-root:Ronald]], [[same-root:Gerald]] and [[same-root:Arnold]].
Shares the ending meaning strong with [[same-root:Harold]].
Shares the ending meaning strong with [[same-root:Harold]].
Shares the ending meaning strong with [[same-root:Harold]].
Noble plus -red, from [[from:rǣdan]], to advise, so roughly well advised; hence Æthelred [[see:unready]] is a pun.
From Old English [[from:rǣdan]], to advise, which is why it is unlike other Germanic languages' words for read.
In Æthelred the Unready it means badly advised, a pun on [[see:Æthelred]], meaning well advised.
Contains the same -ric element, meaning ruler, as [[same-root:Godric]] and [[same-root:Wulfric]].
An Anglo-Saxon name meaning god ruler, with the -ric ending also found in [[same-root:Richard]].
An Anglo-Saxon name meaning wolf ruler, with the -ric ending meaning ruler.
Rob suggests it is related to the -ric element meaning ruler in names like [[same-root?:Godric]].
German word known for notorious reasons, meaning a domain; linked to [[same-root?:rich]] and the -ric in names like Godric.
Ultimately related to the -ric element and [[same-root:rich]], through words for moving in a straight line.
A name in [[see:Beowulf]] that is the Old English version of [[same-root:Roger]]; King Roger sounds less regal.
Spelled with an X instead of CK, an example of parents choosing unusual spellings after looking names up.
Rob saw it spelled unconventionally on an American reality show; also a common name among his classmates.
Means prosperity guard, the -ward meaning to guard; many people nicknamed [[see:Bear]] are Edwards, because of [[see:teddy bear]]s.
A subreddit mocking creatively spelled baby names, named after a real name supposedly given to a child.
Very common in the United States; middle school teachers have more than one per class.
Very common in the United States, like [[see:Aiden]] and [[see:Jaden]].
Very common in the United States, like [[see:Aiden]] and [[see:Braden]].
So common Jess always shared classes with another; first attested in this spelling in Shakespeare's [[see:The Merchant of Venice]] as Shylock's daughter, from a Hebrew word.
A Germanic name meaning will helmet, with many variants, including [[same-root:Wilhelm]], [[same-root:Guillaume]], [[same-root:Bill]] and [[same-root:Liam]].
The German form of [[same-root:William]], in which helm literally means helmet.
Known as [[see:Guillaume]] in French, though Rob thinks in Norman French his name sounded more like Wilhelm.
The French form of [[same-root:William]]; G and W often swap places across languages.
One of the twists on [[same-root:William]].
Surprisingly the same name as [[same-root:Herman]], according to a 1920s US War Department list of names.
Surprisingly the same name as [[same-root:Arminius]].
Has many variants, including [[same-root:Benito]], [[same-root:Bento]] and [[same-root:Bennett]].
A variant of [[same-root:Benedict]].
A variant of [[same-root:Benedict]].
A variant of [[same-root:Benedict]]; the surname Bennett is the same as the surname Benedict.
The same name as [[same-root:Ludwig]], [[same-root:Louis]], [[same-root:Ludovic]], [[same-root:Luigi]] and [[same-root:Clovis]], taken into different languages.
A form of [[same-root:Lewis]].

A form of [[same-root:Lewis]].
The same name as [[same-root:Gautier]], showing the W–G swap seen in William and Guillaume.
The French equivalent of [[same-root:Walter]], as in Jean Paul Gaultier.
A variant of [[same-root:Robert]] in the 1920s War Department list.

A variant of [[same-root:Robert]] listed in the War Department book.
A variant of [[same-root:Robert]]; Jess jokes about calling Rob Bob.
A variant of [[same-root:Robert]] that sounds like a pet name; Rob's dad had a toy called Dobbin the Donkey, then named his son Robert.

A variant of [[same-root:Robert]] listed in the War Department book.
A very old black-and-white British TV show Rob confused with his dad's toy, Dobbin the Donkey, while discussing [[see:Dobbin]].
The same name as [[same-root:George]].
The same name as [[same-root:Jordi]], [[same-root:Jorge]], [[same-root:Jürg]] and [[same-root:Georg]].

The same name as [[same-root:Franco]], [[same-root:Frank]], [[same-root:Frans]] and [[same-root:François]].

A form of [[same-root:Francis]], which people may not realise.

The same name as [[same-root:Esteban]] and [[same-root:Étienne]].
A form of [[same-root:Steven]].
The French form of [[same-root:Steven]].
A biblical name, the same as [[same-root:Jacob]], meaning supplanter or one who takes by the heel, after [[see:Esau]]'s twin being born holding his ankle.
The same name as [[same-root:James]].
A form of [[same-root:James]].

A Gaelic form of [[same-root:James]], the vocative of [[same-root:Seamus]] via [[see:consonant mutation]].
A Gaelic form of [[same-root:James]]; addressed directly in the [[see:vocative case]] it becomes something like [[same-root:Hamish]].
A form of [[same-root:James]].

A form of [[same-root:James]].
A feature of Gaelic and Welsh in which initial consonants change by case, explaining [[see:Seamus]] versus [[see:Hamish]] and the V in [[see:Llanfair]].
The case used to address a person directly, as in poetic 'O Jess'; English lacks one, but Gaelic uses it, giving [[see:Hamish]].
The start of the long Welsh place name Llanfairpwllgwyngyll, meaning church of [[see:Mary]], with M mutated to a V sound.
From Hebrew [[from:Yochanan]], thought to mean God is gracious; its J came from Hebrew Y via Latin I.
The Hebrew source of [[gave:John]] and its European variants, thought to mean God is gracious.
A variant of [[same-root:John]].
A variant of [[same-root:John]].
A variant of [[same-root:John]]; clipped, it gave [[gave:Hans]].
A variant of [[same-root:John]].
A variant of [[same-root:John]].
A variant of [[same-root:John]], which Rob finds interesting.
A variant of [[same-root:John]].
A variant of [[same-root:John]].
A clipped form of [[from:Johannes]], so a variant of John.
In the Bible, his twin was born holding his ankle, explaining the meaning of [[see:James]].
From Hebrew [[from:Miriam]], of uncertain meaning (theories include rebellion, beloved, wished-for child); the top US woman's name of the past century.
The Hebrew source of [[gave:Mary]], [[gave:Marie]], [[gave:Maria]] and [[gave:Maya]].
Etymologically the same name as [[same-root:Mary]].
Etymologically the same name as [[same-root:Mary]].
Etymologically the same name as [[same-root:Mary]].
Second most popular US woman's name of the past century; feminine of [[same-root:Patrick]], from Latin [[from:patricius]], noble, containing the word for father.
The masculine name of which [[same-root:Patricia]] is the feminine form.
Begins with the same pat-, father, as [[same-root:Patricia]].
The Cornish form of [[from:Guinevere]], meaning roughly white, fair or blessed plus phantom or spirit; it became widespread despite Cornish having few speakers.
Latin-origin name meaning worthy of admiration; previously a surname, it became a woman's first name after the character in Shakespeare's The Tempest.
Popularised by Shakespeare; linked to Latin for heart, Welsh [[from?:Creiddylad]], jewel of the sea, or French [[from?:cœur de lion]], heart of a lion.
Virtually unknown until J. M. Barrie's [[see:Peter Pan]], possibly not invented for it, and among Britain's top names by the 1930s.
The name of a Norse god that suddenly entered England and Wales's top five girls' names in 2023, which Rob suspects is due to television.
Became a woman's name after [[see:Florence Nightingale]], named for the city; Rob's French wife finds it strange, since in French Florence is a man's name.
Named after the city where she was born, she popularised [[see:Florence]]; the lady of the lamp worked in Derbyshire, whose hospital bears her name.
A man's name that became a woman's name.
A man's name that became a woman's name.
A name that can still go either way for men and women.
A unisex name; a gag in Community says more Kims are men; Rob's female Kims were all [[see:Kimberly]]s.
A name that can go either way for men and women.
Began as a surname from several place names, meaning something like royal fortress; shortened to [[see:Kim]].
Many women called Charlie are short for [[see:Charlotte]], showing how shortening creates unisex names.
Shortened to [[see:Charlie]], a name shared with men.
Has surprising variants, including [[same-root:Marjorie]], [[same-root:Maggie]], [[same-root:Peggy]], [[see:Daisy]] and [[see:Pearl]], since it means pearl.
A variant of [[same-root:Margaret]].
A variant of [[same-root:Margaret]].
A variant of [[same-root:Margaret]].
A nickname for [[see:Margaret]] because French [[see:marguerite]] names the oxeye daisy; it came up in the hosts' flower episode.
The French name of the oxeye daisy, explaining why [[see:Daisy]] is a nickname for [[same-root:Margaret]].
A nickname for [[see:Margaret]], because Margaret means pearl.
A name seemingly catching on, but many people called Bear are Edwards nicknamed after [[see:teddy bear]]s; compare [[equivalent:Medved]] and [[equivalent:Björn]].
A very famous person called [[see:Bear]].
The reason many Edwards are nicknamed [[see:Bear]].
A Russian name meaning bear, which Rob tried to link to the rise of [[see:Bear]].
A name meaning bear, part of a long European fashion for such names, like [[see:Bear]].
Jess's guess for the top 2024 girls' name; [[see:Betty]] and [[see:Betsy]] are short for it.
The most popular girls' name in England and Wales in 2024 and every year since 2016, and top in the US too.
Second most popular girls' name in England and Wales since 2016, top in 2015, and third in the US.
One of the other popular girls' names in England and Wales.
One of the other popular girls' names in England and Wales.
One of the other popular girls' names in England and Wales.
Long the top boys' name in England and Wales until knocked off two years ago; now third there and third in the US.
Top boys' name in England and Wales; with spellings Mohamed and Mohammed, transliterations of different ages, it has over twice the next name's total.
Second most popular boys' name in England and Wales, and second in the US.
Sometimes given as a surname, but taken by Sikh men on joining the Sikh brotherhood, just as women take [[see:Kaur]].
The name Sikh women take on, the counterpart of [[see:Singh]].
The top US boys' name last year, apparently written as Liam rather than [[from:William]] on birth certificates.
Originally a nickname for [[from:John]], now a name in its own right.
Second most popular US girls' name last year.
Baby-naming idea that parents pick names just old enough not to be grandparents' names, predicting a return of [[see:Susan]] and [[see:Roger]].
Predicted to make a comeback in England in the next generation under the [[see:100-year rule]].
Predicted to make a comeback, though hard to imagine on a baby; [[same-root:Hrothgar]] is its Old English version.
A shortened form of [[from:Elizabeth]] that Jess would be surprised to meet today.
Short for [[from:Elizabeth]], but more US birth certificates in the past century said Betty; popularised by [[see:Betty Grable]], [[see:Betty Boop]] and [[see:Betty White]].
One of the reasons [[see:Betty]] was so popular.
One of the reasons [[see:Betty]] was so popular.
One of the reasons [[see:Betty]] was popular; Jess notes she was born before Martin Luther King Jr.
Rob expects many Margos starting school soon, following the same pop-culture pattern as [[see:Betty]].
The name of the show's third partner; like [[same-root:Marcus]], a [[see:theophoric]] name referencing [[from:Mars]], god of war.
The same name as [[same-root:Martin]], meaning Mars, the Roman god of war.
Describes a name containing a god's name, like [[see:Marcus]], [[see:Heracles]], [[see:Isidora]] and [[see:Nicholas]].
A [[see:theophoric]] name beginning with the goddess [[see:Hera]]'s name.
A [[see:theophoric]] name meaning gift of [[see:Isis]], the Egyptian god.
Long read as bee wolf, a kenning blamed on [[see:J. R. R. Tolkien]]; now widely seen as [[see:theophoric]], with Beow a Germanic god.
Blamed for the bee-wolf reading of [[see:Beowulf]]; his early translation is weak, but his later notes are top Old English analysis.
A [[see:theophoric]] name meaning victory people, whose Nick- is the same as in [[same-root:Nike (goddess)]].
The Greek god of victory, whose name forms the start of [[same-root:Nicholas]].
Essentially the same as [[same-root:barbarian]], from Greek for foreign woman; popularised by [[see:St. Barbara]]; also Jess's aunt, the show's biggest fan.
From Greek for a foreigner, imitating foreign speech heard as 'bar bar'; related to [[same-root:Barbara]].
A 3rd-century Christian martyr whose legend spread across medieval Europe, popularising [[see:Barbara]].
Greek name meaning defender of men, its -ander from [[from:andros]], man, as in [[same-root:androgynous]] and [[same-root:Andrew]].
Contains the same andros, man, as [[same-root:Alexander]].
Contains the same Greek word for man as [[same-root:Alexander]]; it is Jess's spouse's name.
A saint's name from Greek Christophoros, Christ-bearer; saints' names tend to be Greekified, then obscured by Latin.
From St Paul the Apostle, formerly [[see:Saul]] of Tarsus; from Latin [[from:paulus]], small or humble, as he humbled himself.
A form of [[same-root:Paul]].
A form of [[same-root:Paul]].
A form of [[same-root:Paul]].
A form of [[same-root:Paul]].
A form of [[same-root:Paul]].
St Paul's earlier name; changing one letter to become [[see:Paul]] marks his biblical transformation.
Rob compares Saul becoming [[see:Paul]] to these characters, where changing the first letter switches between evil and good.
Famously means stone.
